rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Every electron in an atom carries a four-number address: **n** (principal — shell, size, energy, 2n² capacity), **l** (azimuthal — subshell shape, 0 to n−1: s, p, d, f), **mₗ** (magnetic — orientation, −l to +l, 2l + 1 orbitals per subshell) and **mₛ** (spin — ±1/2, the basis of Pauli's exclusion principle).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - l = 0, 1, 2, …, (n − 1) - mₗ = −l, …, 0, …, +l → orbitals per subshell = 2l + 1 - Max electrons: shell 2n²; subshell 2(2l + 1); orbital 2 - Angular momentum = √(l(l+1))·h/2π

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **l ≤ n − 1, always:** "3f" (n = 3, l = 3) and "2d" (n = 2, l = 2) are impossible — the shape cannot outrun its shell.  ·  **mₗ range depends on l, not n:** mₗ = ±2 is legal only when l ≥ 2 (d or f), whatever n is.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of all four quantum numbers." — Pauli's exclusion principle.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***Fe's last electron: 3, 2, −2, +1/2*** — a 3d electron (n = 3, l = 2); filling starts at mₗ = −2 with spin-up, per Hund's rule and the conventional mₗ ordering.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Verified PYQs: NEB 2024 3m — four quantum numbers of Na's valence electron (solved above); NEB 2023 2m — identify the impossible set (answer b: mₗ = +2 with l = 1). Others are NEB-style practice.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — The Four-Number Address of Every Electron The quantum mechanical model replaced orbits with orbitals; **quantum numbers** are the postal address system that labels each electron inside them. Four numbers — **n, l, mₗ, mₛ** — fix an electron's shell, subshell, orientation and spin. NEB examines them two ways every cycle: *define and give values* (3m) and *test which sets are possible* (2m).…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts — The Four Quantum Numbers ### 2.1 Principal quantum number (n) - **Meaning:** main energy shell; size and energy of the orbital. - **Values:** n = 1, 2, 3, 4, … (K, L, M, N). - **Consequences:** max electrons in a shell = **2n²**; energy rises with n; distance from nucleus rises with n.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "n owns the shell, l owns the shape, mₗ owns the direction, mₛ owns the spin." Values chant: "0 to n−1, minus-l to plus-l, plus or minus a half."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **NEB 2024 (3m): Write the four quantum numbers for the valence electron of sodium (Z = 11).** — Na = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹; the valence electron sits in 3s: **n = 3, l = 0, mₗ = 0, mₛ = +1/2**.  ·  **NEB 2023 (2m): Which set of quantum numbers is not possible: (a) 3, 1, +1, +1/2 (b) 3, 1, +2, −1/2 (c) 3, 1, −1, −1/2 (d) 3, 0, 0, +1/2?** — **(b)**: with l = 1, mₗ may only be −1, 0 or +1; mₗ = +2 violates |mₗ| ≤ l. Sets (a), (c) are legal 3p electrons and (d) is a legal 3s electron.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: For "write the quantum numbers" questions, first write the electron configuration — the address follows mechanically. For "which is impossible", test l against n−1 before anything else; that catches most traps instantly.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Validity checking order:** l against n−1 → mₗ against ±l → mₛ against ±1/2. Run the checks in this order and every "which set is impossible" question resolves mechanically.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: n = shell (1, 2, 3…; 2n² electrons); l = subshell shape (0 to n−1: s, p, d, f); mₗ = orientation (−l to +l, 2l+1 orbitals); mₛ = spin (±1/2). Na valence electron (NEB 2024): n = 3, l = 0, mₗ = 0, mₛ = +1/2. Impossible-set test (NEB 2023): check l ≤ n−1 first, then |mₗ| ≤ l, then mₛ = ±1/2.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Quantum numbers emerged from spectroscopy: Zeeman splitting (mₛ/mₗ) and fine structure could not be explained until each electron needed four coordinates instead of one orbit.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Define the four quantum numbers and state the values each can take.** — **n (principal):** shell, size, energy; 1, 2, 3, … (capacity 2n²). **l (azimuthal):** subshell shape; 0 to n−1, named s, p, d, f. **mₗ (magnetic):** orientation; −l to +l, giving 2l + 1 orbitals.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): An electron has n = 3, l = 2. Give the subshell, the number of orbitals, and all possible mₗ values.** — Subshell **3d**; orbitals = 2l + 1 = **5**; mₗ = **−2, −1, 0, +1, +2**; the subshell holds 10 electrons.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Shell** | All orbitals with the same n | n = 3 is the M shell | | **Subshell** | All orbitals with the same n and l | 3p (n = 3, l = 1) | | **Orbital** | One (n, l, mₗ) state — a probability region | 3p with mₗ = +1 | | **Electron address** | Full set (n, l, mₗ, mₛ) | 3, 1, +1, +1/2 | |…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Worked example — NEB 2024 (3m, verified PYQ) **Q: Write the four quantum numbers for the valence electron of sodium (Z = 11).** Configuration: Na = 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ **3s¹** — the valence electron is in 3s.…  ·  ### Deep dive — the four-number address and its consistency rules Every electron in an atom carries four quantum numbers that act like a postal address, and they must be mutually consistent: - **n** (principal, 1, 2, 3, …) — shell, size and energy; for hydrogen E depends on n alone. - **l** (azimuthal, 0 to n−1) — subshell and shape: s, p, d, f.…

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Why can no subshell hold more than 2(2l + 1) electrons?  ·  Write all four quantum numbers for every electron of helium.  ·  Why does mₗ have no effect on the energy of an orbital in the absence of a magnetic field?

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **The four quantum numbers — ranges, meaning, capacities** | Quantum number | Allowed values | Determines | Capacity rule | |---|---|---|---| | Principal n | 1, 2, 3, … | Shell, size, main energy | Shell holds 2n² electrons | | Azimuthal l | 0 to n−1 (s, p, d, f) | Subshell shape | Subshell holds 2(2l+1)…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables **The four quantum numbers at a glance** | Symbol | Name | Determines | Allowed values | Number of values | |---|---|---|---|---| | **n** | Principal | Shell, size, energy | 1, 2, 3, … | Infinite | | **l** | Azimuthal | Subshell, shape | 0 to n−1 (s, p, d, f) | n per shell | | **mₗ** | Magnetic…  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions **l range vs mₗ range:** l runs **0 to n − 1**; mₗ runs **−l to +l**. For n = 3, l = 2 is legal (3d) but mₗ = 2 with l = 1 is not — the two ranges are different rules.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: **"n = 3, l = 3" trap:** l can never equal n; the highest l in shell n is n − 1 (3f does not exist).  ·  **mₛ values:** only ±1/2 — never ±1. Spin "up/down" is shorthand for the two signs, not a literal direction.  ·  ## 7. Exam Application **NEB-style (2m): How many orbitals and electrons can the M shell hold?** — Orbitals = n² = 9 (one 3s, three 3p, five 3d); electrons = 2n² = **18**.
